subject: living with water shortages in a rural village: buying water, boreholes, tanker queues and giving up on the municipality
citation: Seretlo-Rangata ML, Sodi T, Govender S (2025). Psychological effects of water scarcity on community members: a case study of Lephalale municipality, Limpopo province, South Africa. Frontiers in Psychology 16:1537992. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1537992

claims.text: Extreme scarcity is the baseline: when water is absent for days at a time, any offer is judged against an unbearable, hopeless situation rather than against normal service.
evaluative_rules: Judge any water solution by whether it relieves unbearable scarcity, not by convenience or preference
objections: Will this actually end the days without water, or just add another promise?
vocabulary: how are we supposed to live like this

readings.text: Someone who can go days without access to water might weigh any new water offer mainly by whether it ends that unbearable stretch, not by how it compares to normal service.
If water is absent for days at a time, a new water offer could be judged against an unbearable, hopeless situation, making even a limited offer feel meaningful.
Someone who wonders how they are supposed to live like this might weigh a new water offer as a response to a major water shortage, asking whether it can change a situation that feels unliveable.
If a major water shortage makes life feel unliveable, a new water offer may be judged against that hopeless baseline rather than against normal service.

claims.text: Water access is a money problem: because municipal supply is unreliable, households are forced into costly private alternatives, so any solution is weighed by affordability and the private expenditure it can replace.
evaluative_rules: Weigh a water solution by what it costs against what people are already forced to spend privately
objections: Will this remove the need to pay for water from borehole owners?

readings.text: If buying water from borehole owners on days when government water is unavailable already requires money, a new water solution would be judged by whether it removes that daily need to have money just to get water.
Someone who sees water as very scarce and borehole drilling as very costly but unavoidable would be cautious about any new solution that still depends on private spending.

If people feel they have no choice but to pay for private water, they would still weigh a new solution by its affordability, but might accept it more readily if it clearly replaces the costly alternatives they already use.

claims.text: Scarcity is shameful: because people cannot wash clothes and must queue publicly at tanks, water access is evaluated through dignity and stigma, not just physical need.
evaluative_rules: Judge a water solution by whether it restores dignity and removes public embarrassment
objections: Will this stop me from having to queue in public and go without washing?

readings.text: Someone who feels the shame of not washing clothes may weigh a new water service by whether it lets them avoid that embarrassment.
If waiting in long public queues feels like a shame on us, a new water service may be judged by how much it removes public struggle.
Someone who sees scarcity through dignity may be cautious about any new arrangement that still makes water access visibly scarce.
If water access is evaluated through stigma, a new service could be weighed by whether it makes scarcity less publicly visible.

claims.text: Promises are already broken: because shortages have been reported repeatedly while infrastructure stays behind population growth, any new offer is read through distrust of promises and expectations of unfairness.
evaluative_rules: Judge a water solution by whether it delivers fairly to all villages, not by what authorities promise
objections: Why should I believe this promise when the municipality has already failed us?

readings.text: Someone who has seen promises to help come to nothing would treat any new offer as another promise likely to be broken, and would look first for what could go wrong.
If the struggle has meant travelling long distances to taps that have water, a new offer would be weighed by whether it removes that daily burden, not by what it claims.
Someone who sees population growth outpacing the same size infrastructure would ask whether a new offer actually expands capacity or just adds more users to an already strained system.
If only old villages were supplied with water pipes while new villages were left out, a new offer would be judged by whether it corrects that unfairness or repeats it.

claims.text: Scarce water is contested: because people compete at tanks and communal taps, including with neighboring villages, any new solution is read through conflict risk and whether allocation will be fair.
evaluative_rules: Judge a water solution by whether it prevents fighting and guarantees fair sharing
objections: Will this stop people from stealing taps and using pressure pumps to take more than their share?
vocabulary: this is not fair at all

readings.text: Someone who has seen people fight when government water tanks arrive would judge any new solution first by whether it removes the need to compete at the point of delivery.
If people steal communal taps that help the whole community, a new solution would be weighed by how easily its parts can be taken or broken by one person.
Someone who is irritated that pressure pumps let some people take water before others would look more favourably on a new solution that stops one household using up the shared supply first.

If people from neighbouring villages come to use street taps when there is water, a new solution would be read through whether it makes the boundary between who is allowed to draw water and who is not clearer.

confidence: qualitative case study, single municipality, fieldwork around 2014 — mechanisms durable, magnitudes unknown
year_note: Interviews October 2020 to April 2021, Ga-Seleka village, Lephalale (Limpopo); participants aged 40-60.
